docs\models\index.md:214:### Ways to integrate non-OpenAI providers

docs\models\index.md:223:You can integrate other LLM providers with these built-in paths:
docs\models\index.md:225:1. [`set_default_openai_client`][agents.set_default_openai_client] is useful in cases where you want to globally use an instance of `AsyncOpenAI` as the LLM client. docs\models\index.md:244:    In these examples, we use the Chat Completions API/model, because many LLM providers still do not support the Responses API. If your LLM provider does support it, we recommend using Responses.
docs\models\index.md:256:    While our SDK supports both the [`OpenAIResponsesModel`][agents.models.openai_responses.OpenAIResponsesModel] and the [`OpenAIChatCompletionsModel`][agents.models.openai_chatcompletions.OpenAIChatCompletionsModel] shapes, we recommend using a single model shape for each workflow because the two shapes support a different set of features and tools. docs\models\index.md:305:## Advanced OpenAI Responses settings
docs\models\index.md:307:When you are on the OpenAI Responses path and need more control, start with `ModelSettings`.
docs\models\index.md:311:When you are using the OpenAI Responses API, several request fields already have direct `ModelSettings` fields, so you do not need `extra_args` for them.
docs\models\index.md:314:- `truncation`: Set `"auto"` to let the Responses API drop the oldest conversation items instead of failing when context would overflow.
docs\models\index.md:316:- `context_management`: Configure server-side context handling such as Responses compaction with `compact_threshold`.
docs\models\index.md:340:When you set `store=False`, the Responses API does not keep that response available for later server-side retrieval. This is useful for stateless or zero-data-retention style flows, but it also means features that would otherwise reuse response IDs need to rely on locally managed state instead. For example, [`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession`][agents.memory.openai_responses_compaction_session.OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession] switches its default `"auto"` compaction path to input-based compaction when the last response was not stored. See the [Sessions guide](../sessions/index.md#openai-responses-compaction-sessions).
docs\models\index.md:342:Server-side compaction is different from [`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession`][agents.memory.openai_responses_compaction_session.OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession]. `context_management=[{"type": "compaction", "compact_threshold": ...}]` is sent with each Responses API request, and the API can emit compaction items as part of the response when the rendered context crosses the threshold. `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` calls the standalone `responses.compact` endpoint between turns and rewrites the local session history.
docs\models\index.md:346:Use `extra_args` when you need provider-specific or newer request fields that the SDK does not expose directly at the top level yet.
docs\models\index.md:348:Also, when you use OpenAI's Responses API, [there are a few other optional parameters](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/responses/create) (e.g., `user`, `service_tier`, and so on). If they are not available at the top level, you can use `extra_args` to pass them as well. Do not also set the same request field through a direct `ModelSettings` field.
docs\models\index.md:384:                retry_policies.provider_suggested(),
docs\models\index.md:412:- `provider_advice` when the underlying model adapter can supply retry guidance.
docs\models\index.md:424:| `retry_policies.provider_suggested()` | Follows provider retry advice when available. |
docs\models\index.md:431:When you compose policies, `provider_suggested()` is the safest first building block because it preserves provider vetoes and replay-safety approvals when the provider can distinguish them.
docs\models\index.md:438:- Requests where provider advice marks replay as unsafe.
docs\models\index.md:441:Stateful follow-up requests using `previous_response_id` or `conversation_id` are also treated more conservatively. For those requests, non-provider predicates such as `network_error()` or `http_status([500])` are not enough by themselves. The retry policy should include a replay-safe approval from the provider, typically via `retry_policies.provider_suggested()`.
docs\models\index.md:451:For fuller examples, see [`examples/basic/retry.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/basic/retry.py) and the [adapter-backed retry example](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/basic/retry_litellm.py).

docs\models\index.md:482:## Mixing models across providers
docs\models\index.md:484:You need to be aware of feature differences between model providers, or you may run into errors. For example, OpenAI supports structured outputs, multimodal input, and hosted file search and web search, but many other providers don't support these features. Be aware of these limitations:
docs\models\index.md:486:-   Don't send unsupported `tools` to providers that don't understand them
docs\models\index.md:488:-   Be aware that providers that don't support structured JSON outputs will occasionally produce invalid JSON.
docs\models\index.md:492:Reach for a third-party adapter only when the SDK's built-in provider integration points are not enough. If you are using OpenAI models only with this SDK, prefer the built-in [`OpenAIResponsesModel`][agents.models.openai_responses.OpenAIResponsesModel] path instead of Any-LLM or LiteLLM. Third-party adapters are for cases where you need to combine OpenAI models with non-OpenAI providers, or need adapter-managed provider coverage or routing that the built-in paths do not provide. Adapters add another compatibility layer between the SDK and the upstream model provider, so feature support and request semantics can vary by provider. The SDK currently includes Any-LLM and LiteLLM as best-effort, beta adapter integrations.
docs\models\index.md:496:Any-LLM support is included on a best-effort, beta basis for cases where you need Any-LLM-managed provider coverage or routing.
docs\models\index.md:498:Depending on the upstream provider path, Any-LLM may use the Responses API, Chat Completions-compatible APIs, or provider-specific compatibility layers.
docs\models\index.md:500:If you need Any-LLM, install `openai-agents[any-llm]`, then start from [`examples/model_providers/any_llm_auto.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/any_llm_auto.py) or [`examples/model_providers/any_llm_provider.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/any_llm_provider.py). You can use `any-llm/...` model names with [`MultiProvider`][agents.MultiProvider], instantiate `AnyLLMModel` directly, or use `AnyLLMProvider` at run scope. If you need to pin the model surface explicitly, pass `api="responses"` or `api="chat_completions"` when constructing `AnyLLMModel`.
docs\models\index.md:502:Any-LLM remains a third-party adapter layer, so provider dependencies and capability gaps are defined upstream by Any-LLM rather than by the SDK. Usage metrics are propagated automatically when the upstream provider returns them, but streamed Chat Completions backends may require `ModelSettings(include_usage=True)` before they emit usage chunks. Validate the exact provider backend you plan to deploy if you depend on structured outputs, tool calling, usage reporting, or Responses-specific behavior.
docs\models\index.md:504:### LiteLLM
docs\models\index.md:506:LiteLLM support is included on a best-effort, beta basis for cases where you need LiteLLM-specific provider coverage or routing.

docs\tracing.md:3:The Agents SDK includes built-in tracing, collecting a comprehensive record of events during an agent run: LLM generations, tool calls, handoffs, guardrails, and even custom events that occur. Using the [Traces dashboard](https://platform.openai.com/traces), you can debug, visualize, and monitor your workflows during development and in production.
docs\tracing.md:15:## Traces and spans
docs\tracing.md:17:-   **Traces** represent a single end-to-end operation of a "workflow". They're composed of Spans. Traces have the following properties:
docs\tracing.md:19:    -   `trace_id`: A unique ID for the trace. Automatically generated if you don't pass one. Must have the format `trace_<32_alphanumeric>`.
docs\tracing.md:20:    -   `group_id`: Optional group ID, to link multiple traces from the same conversation. For example, you might use a chat thread ID.
docs\tracing.md:21:    -   `disabled`: If True, the trace will not be recorded.
docs\tracing.md:22:    -   `metadata`: Optional metadata for the trace.
docs\tracing.md:25:    -   `trace_id`, to represent the trace they belong to
docs\tracing.md:27:    -   `span_data`, which is information about the Span. For example, `AgentSpanData` contains information about the Agent, `GenerationSpanData` contains information about the LLM generation, etc.
docs\tracing.md:31:By default, the SDK traces the following:
docs\tracing.md:33:-   The entire `Runner.{run, run_sync, run_streamed}()` is wrapped in a `trace()`.
docs\tracing.md:34:-   Each time an agent runs, it is wrapped in `agent_span()`
docs\tracing.md:35:-   LLM generations are wrapped in `generation_span()`
docs\tracing.md:36:-   Function tool calls are each wrapped in `function_span()`
docs\tracing.md:37:-   Guardrails are wrapped in `guardrail_span()`
docs\tracing.md:38:-   Handoffs are wrapped in `handoff_span()`
docs\tracing.md:39:-   Audio inputs (speech-to-text) are wrapped in a `transcription_span()`
docs\tracing.md:40:-   Audio outputs (text-to-speech) are wrapped in a `speech_span()`
docs\tracing.md:41:-   Related audio spans may be parented under a `speech_group_span()`
docs\tracing.md:43:By default, the trace is named "Agent workflow". You can set this name if you use `trace`, or you can configure the name and other properties with the [`RunConfig`][agents.run.RunConfig].
docs\tracing.md:45:In addition, you can set up [custom trace processors](#custom-tracing-processors) to push traces to other destinations (as a replacement, or secondary destination).
docs\tracing.md:49:The default [`BatchTraceProcessor`][agents.tracing.processors.BatchTraceProcessor] exports traces
docs\tracing.md:52:RQ, Dramatiq, or FastAPI background tasks, this means traces are usually exported automatically
docs\tracing.md:53:without any extra code, but they may not appear in the Traces dashboard immediately after each job
docs\tracing.md:57:[`flush_traces()`][agents.tracing.flush_traces] after the trace context exits.
docs\tracing.md:60:from agents import Runner, flush_traces, trace

docs\tracing.md:94:[`flush_traces()`][agents.tracing.flush_traces] blocks until currently buffered traces and spans are
docs\tracing.md:95:exported, so call it after `trace()` closes to avoid flushing a partially built trace. You can skip
docs\tracing.md:98:## Higher level traces
docs\tracing.md:100:Sometimes, you might want multiple calls to `run()` to be part of a single trace. You can do this by wrapping the entire code in a `trace()`.
docs\tracing.md:103:from agents import Agent, Runner, trace
docs\tracing.md:108:    with trace("Joke workflow"): # (1)!
docs\tracing.md:115:1. Because the two calls to `Runner.run` are wrapped in a `with trace()`, the individual runs will be part of the overall trace rather than creating two traces.
docs\tracing.md:117:## Creating traces
docs\tracing.md:119:You can use the [`trace()`][agents.tracing.trace] function to create a trace. Traces need to be started and finished. You have two options to do so:
docs\tracing.md:121:1. **Recommended**: use the trace as a context manager, i.e. `with trace(...) as my_trace`. This will automatically start and end the trace at the right time.
docs\tracing.md:122:2. You can also manually call [`trace.start()`][agents.tracing.Trace.start] and [`trace.finish()`][agents.tracing.Trace.finish].
docs\tracing.md:124:The current trace is tracked via a Python [`contextvar`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextvars.html). This means that it works with concurrency automatically. If you manually start/end a trace, you'll need to pass `mark_as_current` and `reset_current` to `start()`/`finish()` to update the current trace.
docs\tracing.md:126:## Creating spans
docs\tracing.md:128:You can use the various [`*_span()`][agents.tracing.create] methods to create a span. In general, you don't need to manually create spans. A [`custom_span()`][agents.tracing.custom_span] function is available for tracking custom span information.
docs\tracing.md:130:Spans are automatically part of the current trace, and are nested under the nearest current span, which is tracked via a Python [`contextvar`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextvars.html).
docs\tracing.md:134:Certain spans may capture potentially sensitive data.
docs\tracing.md:136:The `generation_span()` stores the inputs/outputs of the LLM generation, and `function_span()` stores the inputs/outputs of function calls. These may contain sensitive data, so you can disable capturing that data via [`RunConfig.trace_include_sensitive_data`][agents.run.RunConfig.trace_include_sensitive_data].
docs\tracing.md:138:Similarly, Audio spans include base64-encoded PCM data for input and output audio by default. You can disable capturing this audio data by configuring [`VoicePipelineConfig.trace_include_sensitive_audio_data`][agents.voice.pipeline_config.VoicePipelineConfig.trace_include_sensitive_audio_data].
docs\tracing.md:140:By default, `trace_include_sensitive_data` is `True`. You can set the default without code by exporting the `OPENAI_AGENTS_TRACE_INCLUDE_SENSITIVE_DATA` environment variable to `true/1` or `false/0` before running your app.
docs\tracing.md:146:-   At initialization, we create a global [`TraceProvider`][agents.tracing.setup.TraceProvider], which is responsible for creating traces.
docs\tracing.md:147:-   We configure the `TraceProvider` with a [`BatchTraceProcessor`][agents.tracing.processors.BatchTraceProcessor] that sends traces/spans in batches to a [`BackendSpanExporter`][agents.tracing.processors.BackendSpanExporter], which exports the spans and traces to the OpenAI backend in batches.
docs\tracing.md:149:To customize this default setup, to send traces to alternative or additional backends or modifying exporter behavior, you have two options:
docs\tracing.md:151:1. [`add_trace_processor()`][agents.tracing.add_trace_processor] lets you add an **additional** trace processor that will receive traces and spans as they are ready. This lets you do your own processing in addition to sending traces to OpenAI's backend.
docs\tracing.md:152:2. [`set_trace_processors()`][agents.tracing.set_trace_processors] lets you **replace** the default processors with your own trace processors. This means traces will not be sent to the OpenAI backend unless you include a `TracingProcessor` that does so.
docs\tracing.md:157:You can use an OpenAI API key with non-OpenAI models to enable free tracing in the OpenAI Traces dashboard without needing to disable tracing. See the [Third-party adapters](models/index.md#third-party-adapters) section in the Models guide for adapter selection and setup caveats.

docs\models\index.md:492:Reach for a third-party adapter only when the SDK's built-in provider integration points are not enough. If you are using OpenAI models only with this SDK, prefer the built-in [`OpenAIResponsesModel`][agents.models.openai_responses.OpenAIResponsesModel] path instead of Any-LLM or LiteLLM. Third-party adapters are for cases where you need to combine OpenAI models with non-OpenAI providers, or need adapter-managed provider coverage or routing that the built-in paths do not provide. Adapters add another compatibility layer between the SDK and the upstream model provider, so feature support and request semantics can vary by provider. The SDK currently includes Any-LLM and LiteLLM as best-effort, beta adapter integrations.
docs\models\index.md:496:Any-LLM support is included on a best-effort, beta basis for cases where you need Any-LLM-managed provider coverage or routing.
docs\models\index.md:506:LiteLLM support is included on a best-effort, beta basis for cases where you need LiteLLM-specific provider coverage or routing.
docs\models\index.md:510:Some LiteLLM-backed providers do not populate SDK usage metrics by default. If you need usage reporting, pass `ModelSettings(include_usage=True)` and validate the exact provider backend you plan to deploy if you depend on structured outputs, tool calling, usage reporting, or adapter-specific routing behavior.

docs\models\index.md:340:When you set `store=False`, the Responses API does not keep that response available for later server-side retrieval. This is useful for stateless or zero-data-retention style flows, but it also means features that would otherwise reuse response IDs need to rely on locally managed state instead. For example, [`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession`][agents.memory.openai_responses_compaction_session.OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession] switches its default `"auto"` compaction path to input-based compaction when the last response was not stored. See the [Sessions guide](../sessions/index.md#openai-responses-compaction-sessions).
docs\models\index.md:342:Server-side compaction is different from [`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession`][agents.memory.openai_responses_compaction_session.OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession]. `context_management=[{"type": "compaction", "compact_threshold": ...}]` is sent with each Responses API request, and the API can emit compaction items as part of the response when the rendered context crosses the threshold. `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` calls the standalone `responses.compact` endpoint between turns and rewrites the local session history.

docs\models\index.md:492:Reach for a third-party adapter only when the SDK's built-in provider integration points are not enough. If you are using OpenAI models only with this SDK, prefer the built-in [`OpenAIResponsesModel`][agents.models.openai_responses.OpenAIResponsesModel] path instead of Any-LLM or LiteLLM. Third-party adapters are for cases where you need to combine OpenAI models with non-OpenAI providers, or need adapter-managed provider coverage or routing that the built-in paths do not provide. 270:class Agent(AgentBase, Generic[TContext]):
271:    """An agent is an AI model configured with instructions, tools, guardrails, handoffs and more.
272:
273:    We strongly recommend passing `instructions`, which is the "system prompt" for the agent. In
274:    addition, you can pass `handoff_description`, which is a human-readable description of the
275:    agent, used when the agent is used inside tools/handoffs.
276:
277:    Agents are generic on the context type. The context is a (mutable) object you create. It is
278:    passed to tool functions, handoffs, guardrails, etc.
279:
280:    See `AgentBase` for base parameters that are shared with `RealtimeAgent`s.
281:    """
282:

286:            [RunContextWrapper[TContext], Agent[TContext]],
287:            MaybeAwaitable[str],
288:        ]
289:        | None
290:    ) = None
291:    """The instructions for the agent. Will be used as the "system prompt" when this agent is
292:    invoked. Describes what the agent should do, and how it responds.
293:
294:    Can either be a string, or a function that dynamically generates instructions for the agent. If
295:    you provide a function, it will be called with the context and the agent instance. It must
296:    return a string.
297:    """
298:
299:    prompt: Prompt | DynamicPromptFunction | None = None

303:    """

308:    modularity.
309:    """

316:    """

335:    You can customize this in two ways:
336:    1. If you want non-strict schemas, pass `AgentOutputSchema(MyClass, strict_json_schema=False)`.
337:    2. If you want to use a custom JSON schema (i.e. without using the SDK's automatic schema)
338:       creation, subclass and pass an `AgentOutputSchemaBase` subclass.

346:        Literal["run_llm_again", "stop_on_first_tool"] | StopAtTools | ToolsToFinalOutputFunction
347:    ) = "run_llm_again"
348:    """
349:    This lets you configure how tool use is handled.
350:    - "run_llm_again": The default behavior. Tools are run, and then the LLM receives the results
351:        and gets to respond.
352:    - "stop_on_first_tool": The output from the first tool call is treated as the final result.
353:        In other words, it isn’t sent back to the LLM for further processing but is used directly
354:        as the final output.
355:    - A StopAtTools object: The agent will stop running if any of the tools listed in
356:        `stop_at_tool_names` is called.
357:        The final output will be the output of the first matching tool call.
358:        The LLM does not process the result of the tool call.
359:    - A function: If you pass a function, it will be called with the run context and the list of
360:      tool results. It must return a `ToolsToFinalOutputResult`, which determines whether the tool
520:        hooks: RunHooks[TContext] | None = None,

529:        include_input_schema: bool = False,
530:    ) -> FunctionTool:
531:        """Transform this agent into a tool, callable by other agents.
532:
533:        This is different from handoffs in two ways:
534:        1. In handoffs, the new agent receives the conversation history. In this tool, the new agent
535:           receives generated input.
536:        2. In handoffs, the new agent takes over the conversation. In this tool, the new agent is
537:           called as a tool, and the conversation is continued by the original agent.
538:
539:        Args:
540:            tool_name: The name of the tool. If not provided, the agent's name will be used.
541:            tool_description: The description of the tool, which should indicate what it does and
542:                when to use it.

545:                `agent_tool_invocation` metadata when this agent is invoked via `as_tool()`.

547:                context and agent and returns whether the tool is enabled. Disabled tools are hidden
548:                from the LLM at runtime.
549:            on_stream: Optional callback (sync or async) to receive streaming events from the nested
550:                agent run. The callback receives an `AgentToolStreamEvent` containing the nested
551:                agent, the originating tool call (when available), and each stream event. When
552:                provided, the nested agent is executed in streaming mode.
553:            failure_error_function: If provided, generate an error message when the tool (agent) run
554:                fails. The message is sent to the LLM. If None, the exception is raised instead.
555:            needs_approval: Bool or callable to decide if this agent tool should pause for approval.
556:            parameters: Structured input type for the tool arguments (dataclass or Pydantic model).
557:            input_builder: Optional function to build the nested agent input from structured data.
558:            include_input_schema: Whether to include the full JSON schema in structured input.
559:        """

18:    """A map of model name prefixes to ModelProviders."""

20:    def __init__(self):
21:        self._mapping: dict[str, ModelProvider] = {}

24:        """Returns True if the given prefix is in the mapping."""
25:        return prefix in self._mapping
26:

28:        """Returns a copy of the current prefix -> ModelProvider mapping."""
29:        return self._mapping.copy()
30:
31:    def set_mapping(self, mapping: dict[str, ModelProvider]):
32:        """Overwrites the current mapping with a new one."""
33:        self._mapping = mapping

36:        """Returns the ModelProvider for the given prefix.
37:
38:        Args:
39:            prefix: The prefix of the model name e.g. "openai" or "my_prefix".
40:        """

44:        """Adds a new prefix -> ModelProvider mapping.

46:        Args:
47:            prefix: The prefix of the model name e.g. "openai" or "my_prefix".
48:            provider: The ModelProvider to use for the given prefix.
49:        """

61:class MultiProvider(ModelProvider):
62:    """This ModelProvider maps to a Model based on the prefix of the model name. By default, the
63:    mapping is:
64:    - "openai/" prefix or no prefix -> OpenAIProvider. e.g. "openai/gpt-4.1", "gpt-4.1"
65:    - "litellm/" prefix -> LitellmProvider. e.g. "litellm/openai/gpt-4.1"
66:    - "any-llm/" prefix -> AnyLLMProvider. e.g. "any-llm/openrouter/openai/gpt-4.1"
67:
68:    You can override or customize this mapping. The ``openai`` prefix is ambiguous for some
69:    OpenAI-compatible backends because a string like ``openai/gpt-4.1`` could mean either "route
70:    to the OpenAI provider and use model ``gpt-4.1``" or "send the literal model ID
71:    ``openai/gpt-4.1`` to the configured OpenAI-compatible endpoint." The prefix mode options let
72:    callers opt into the second behavior without breaking the historical alias semantics.
73:    """

102:                use the default base URL.

104:                OpenAI client using the api_key and base_url.
105:            openai_organization: The organization to use for the OpenAI provider.
106:            openai_project: The project to use for the OpenAI provider.
107:            openai_use_responses: Whether to use the OpenAI responses API.
108:            openai_use_responses_websocket: Whether to use websocket transport for the OpenAI
109:                responses API.
110:            openai_strict_feature_validation: Whether OpenAI Chat Completions models should raise
111:                a UserError when callers pass Responses-only features such as previous_response_id,
112:                conversation_id, or prompt. Defaults to False, which preserves the previous
113:                ignore-and-warn behavior.

117:                ``"alias"`` preserves the historical behavior and strips the ``openai/`` prefix

123:                the OpenAI provider so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can receive namespaced model IDs
124:                such as ``openrouter/openai/gpt-4o``.
125:            openai_agent_registration: Optional agent registration configuration for the OpenAI
126:                provider.

636:    def _fix_tool_message_ordering(
637:        self, messages: list[ChatCompletionMessageParam]
638:    ) -> list[ChatCompletionMessageParam]:
639:        """
640:        Fix the ordering of tool messages to ensure tool_use messages come before tool_result messages.
641:
642:        Required for Anthropic and Vertex AI Gemini APIs which require tool calls to immediately
643:        precede their corresponding tool responses in conversation history.
644:        """  # noqa: E501
645:        if not messages:
646:            return messages
647:
648:        # Collect all tool calls and tool results
649:        tool_call_messages = {}  # tool_id -> (index, message)
650:        tool_result_messages = {}  # tool_id -> (index, message)
651:        other_messages = []  # (index, message) for non-tool messages
652:
653:        for i, message in enumerate(messages):
654:            if not isinstance(message, dict):
655:                other_messages.append((i, message))
656:                continue
657:
658:            role = message.get("role")
659:
660:            if role == "assistant" and message.get("tool_calls"):
661:                # Extract tool calls from this assistant message

663:                if isinstance(tool_calls, list):
664:                    for split_idx, tool_call in enumerate(tool_calls):
665:                        if isinstance(tool_call, dict):
666:                            tool_id = tool_call.get("id")
667:                            if tool_id:
668:                                # Create a separate assistant message for each tool call.
669:                                # Only the first split keeps the assistant text/thinking
670:                                # blocks/reasoning content; the rest carry tool_calls only,
671:                                # to avoid duplicating signed thinking blocks (which
672:                                # Anthropic rejects) and assistant text in history.
673:                                single_tool_msg = cast(dict[str, Any], message.copy())
674:                                single_tool_msg["tool_calls"] = [tool_call]
675:                                if split_idx > 0:

677:                                        "content",
678:                                        "thinking_blocks",
679:                                        "reasoning_content",
680:                                    ):
681:                                        single_tool_msg.pop(shared_field, None)
682:                                tool_call_messages[tool_id] = (

684:                                    cast(ChatCompletionMessageParam, single_tool_msg),

212:If you need a non-OpenAI provider, start with the SDK's built-in provider integration points. In many setups, this is enough without adding a third-party adapter. Examples for each pattern live in [examples/model_providers](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/).
213:
214:### Ways to integrate non-OpenAI providers
215:
216:| Approach | Use it when | Scope |
217:| --- | --- | --- |
218:| [`set_default_openai_client`][agents.set_default_openai_client] | One OpenAI-compatible endpoint should be the default for most or all agents | Global default |
219:| [`ModelProvider`][agents.models.interface.ModelProvider] | One custom provider should apply to a single run | Per run |
220:| [`Agent.model`][agents.agent.Agent.model] | Different agents need different providers or concrete model objects | Per agent |
221:| Third-party adapter | You need adapter-managed provider coverage or routing that the built-in paths do not provide | See [Third-party adapters](#third-party-adapters) |
222:
223:You can integrate other LLM providers with these built-in paths:
224:
225:1. [`set_default_openai_client`][agents.set_default_openai_client] is useful in cases where you want to globally use an instance of `AsyncOpenAI` as the LLM client. This is for cases where the LLM provider has an OpenAI compatible API endpoint, and you can set the `base_url` and `api_key`. See a configurable example in [examples/model_providers/custom_example_global.py](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/custom_example_global.py).
226:2. [`ModelProvider`][agents.models.interface.ModelProvider] is at the `Runner.run` level. This lets you say "use a custom model provider for all agents in this run". See a configurable example in [examples/model_providers/custom_example_provider.py](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/custom_example_provider.py).
227:3. [`Agent.model`][agents.agent.Agent.model] lets you specify the model on a specific Agent instance. This enables you to mix and match different providers for different agents. See a configurable example in [examples/model_providers/custom_example_agent.py](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/custom_example_agent.py).
228:
229:In cases where you do not have an API key from `platform.openai.com`, we recommend disabling tracing via `set_tracing_disabled()`, or setting up a [different tracing processor](../tracing.md).
230:
231:``` python
232:from agents import Agent, AsyncOpenAI, OpenAIChatCompletionsModel, set_tracing_disabled
233:
234:set_tracing_disabled(disabled=True)
235:
236:client = AsyncOpenAI(api_key="Api_Key", base_url="Base URL of Provider")
237:model = OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(model="Model_Name", openai_client=client)
238:
239:agent= Agent(name="Helping Agent", instructions="You are a Helping Agent", model=model)
240:```
241:
242:!!! note
243:
244:    In these examples, we use the Chat Completions API/model, because many LLM providers still do not support the Responses API. If your LLM provider does support it, we recommend using Responses.
245:
246:## Mixing models in one workflow
247:
248:Within a single workflow, you may want to use different models for each agent. For example, you could use a smaller, faster model for triage, while using a larger, more capable model for complex tasks. When configuring an [`Agent`][agents.Agent], you can select a specific model by either:
249:
250:1. Passing the name of a model.
251:2. Passing any model name + a [`ModelProvider`][agents.models.interface.ModelProvider] that can map that name to a Model instance.
252:3. Directly providing a [`Model`][agents.models.interface.Model] implementation.
253:
254:!!! note
255:
256:    While our SDK supports both the [`OpenAIResponsesModel`][agents.models.openai_responses.OpenAIResponsesModel] and the [`OpenAIChatCompletionsModel`][agents.models.openai_chatcompletions.OpenAIChatCompletionsModel] shapes, we recommend using a single model shape for each workflow because the two shapes support a different set of features and tools. If your workflow requires mixing and matching model shapes, make sure that all the features you're using are available on both.

258:```python
259:from agents import Agent, Runner, AsyncOpenAI, OpenAIChatCompletionsModel
260:import asyncio
453:## Troubleshooting non-OpenAI providers
454:
455:### Tracing client error 401
456:
457:If you get errors related to tracing, this is because traces are uploaded to OpenAI servers, and you don't have an OpenAI API key. You have three options to resolve this:
458:
459:1. Disable tracing entirely: [`set_tracing_disabled(True)`][agents.set_tracing_disabled].
460:2. Set an OpenAI key for tracing: [`set_tracing_export_api_key(...)`][agents.set_tracing_export_api_key]. This API key will only be used for uploading traces, and must be from [platform.openai.com](https://platform.openai.com/).
461:3. Use a non-OpenAI trace processor. See the [tracing docs](../tracing.md#custom-tracing-processors).
462:
463:### Responses API support
464:
465:The SDK uses the Responses API by default, but many other LLM providers still do not support it. You may see 404s or similar issues as a result. To resolve, you have two options:
466:
467:1. Call [`set_default_openai_api("chat_completions")`][agents.set_default_openai_api]. This works if you are setting `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_BASE_URL` via environment vars.
468:2. Use [`OpenAIChatCompletionsModel`][agents.models.openai_chatcompletions.OpenAIChatCompletionsModel]. There are examples [here](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/).
469:
470:### Structured outputs support
471:
472:Some model providers don't have support for [structured outputs](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs). This sometimes results in an error that looks something like this:
473:
474:```
475:
476:BadRequestError: Error code: 400 - {'error': {'message': "'response_format.type' : value is not one of the allowed values ['text','json_object']", 'type': 'invalid_request_error'}}
477:
478:```
479:
480:This is a shortcoming of some model providers - they support JSON outputs, but don't allow you to specify the `json_schema` to use for the output. We are working on a fix for this, but we suggest relying on providers that do have support for JSON schema output, because otherwise your app will often break because of malformed JSON.
481:
482:## Mixing models across providers
483:
484:You need to be aware of feature differences between model providers, or you may run into errors. For example, OpenAI supports structured outputs, multimodal input, and hosted file search and web search, but many other providers don't support these features. Be aware of these limitations:
485:
486:-   Don't send unsupported `tools` to providers that don't understand them
487:-   Filter out multimodal inputs before calling models that are text-only
488:-   Be aware that providers that don't support structured JSON outputs will occasionally produce invalid JSON.
489:
490:## Third-party adapters
491:
492:Reach for a third-party adapter only when the SDK's built-in provider integration points are not enough. If you are using OpenAI models only with this SDK, prefer the built-in [`OpenAIResponsesModel`][agents.models.openai_responses.OpenAIResponsesModel] path instead of Any-LLM or LiteLLM. Third-party adapters are for cases where you need to combine OpenAI models with non-OpenAI providers, or need adapter-managed provider coverage or routing that the built-in paths do not provide. Adapters add another compatibility layer between the SDK and the upstream model provider, so feature support and request semantics can vary by provider. The SDK currently includes Any-LLM and LiteLLM as best-effort, beta adapter integrations.
493:
494:### Any-LLM
495:
496:Any-LLM support is included on a best-effort, beta basis for cases where you need Any-LLM-managed provider coverage or routing.
497:
498:Depending on the upstream provider path, Any-LLM may use the Responses API, Chat Completions-compatible APIs, or provider-specific compatibility layers.
499:
500:If you need Any-LLM, install `openai-agents[any-llm]`, then start from [`examples/model_providers/any_llm_auto.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/any_llm_auto.py) or [`examples/model_providers/any_llm_provider.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/any_llm_provider.py). You can use `any-llm/...` model names with [`MultiProvider`][agents.MultiProvider], instantiate `AnyLLMModel` directly, or use `AnyLLMProvider` at run scope. If you need to pin the model surface explicitly, pass `api="responses"` or `api="chat_completions"` when constructing `AnyLLMModel`.
501:
502:Any-LLM remains a third-party adapter layer, so provider dependencies and capability gaps are defined upstream by Any-LLM rather than by the SDK. Usage metrics are propagated automatically when the upstream provider returns them, but streamed Chat Completions backends may require `ModelSettings(include_usage=True)` before they emit usage chunks. Validate the exact provider backend you plan to deploy if you depend on structured outputs, tool calling, usage reporting, or Responses-specific behavior.
503:
504:### LiteLLM
505:
506:LiteLLM support is included on a best-effort, beta basis for cases where you need LiteLLM-specific provider coverage or routing.
507:
508:If you need LiteLLM, install `openai-agents[litellm]`, then start from [`examples/model_providers/litellm_auto.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/litellm_auto.py) or [`examples/model_providers/litellm_provider.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/model_providers/litellm_provider.py). You can use `litellm/...` model names or instantiate [`LitellmModel`][agents.extensions.models.litellm_model.LitellmModel] directly.
509:
510:Some LiteLLM-backed providers do not populate SDK usage metrics by default. If you need usage reporting, pass `ModelSettings(include_usage=True)` and validate the exact provider backend you plan to deploy if you depend on structured outputs, tool calling, usage reporting, or adapter-specific routing behavior.

1:# Quickstart
2:
3:!!! warning "Beta feature"
4:
5:    Sandbox agents are in beta. Expect details of the API, defaults, and supported capabilities to change before general availability, and expect more advanced features over time.
6:
7:Modern agents work best when they can operate on real files in a filesystem. **Sandbox Agents** in the Agents SDK give the model a persistent workspace where it can search large document sets, edit files, run commands, generate artifacts, and pick work back up from saved sandbox state.
8:
9:The SDK gives you that execution harness without making you wire together file staging, filesystem tools, shell access, sandbox lifecycle, snapshots, and provider-specific glue yourself. You keep the normal `Agent` and `Runner` flow, then add a `Manifest` for the workspace, capabilities for sandbox-native tools, and `SandboxRunConfig` for where the work runs.
10:
11:## Prerequisites
12:
13:- Python 3.10 or higher
14:- Basic familiarity with the OpenAI Agents SDK
15:- A sandbox client. For local development, start with `UnixLocalSandboxClient`.
16:
17:## Installation
18:
19:If you have not already installed the SDK:
20:
21:```bash
22:pip install openai-agents
23:```
24:
25:For Docker-backed sandboxes:
26:
27:```bash
28:pip install "openai-agents[docker]"
29:```
30:
31:## Create a local sandbox agent
32:
33:This example stages a local repo under `repo/`, loads local skills lazily, and lets the runner create a Unix-local sandbox session for the run.
34:
35:```python
36:import asyncio
37:from pathlib import Path
38:
39:from agents import Runner
40:from agents.run import RunConfig
41:from agents.sandbox import Manifest, SandboxAgent, SandboxRunConfig
42:from agents.sandbox.capabilities import Capabilities, LocalDirLazySkillSource, Skills
43:from agents.sandbox.entries import LocalDir
44:from agents.sandbox.sandboxes.unix_local import UnixLocalSandboxClient
45:
46:EXAMPLE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
47:HOST_REPO_DIR = EXAMPLE_DIR / "repo"
48:HOST_SKILLS_DIR = EXAMPLE_DIR / "skills"
49:
50:
51:def build_agent(model: str) -> SandboxAgent[None]:
52:    return SandboxAgent(
53:        name="Sandbox engineer",
54:        model=model,
55:        instructions=(
56:            "Read `repo/task.md` before editing files. Stay grounded in the repository, preserve "
57:            "existing behavior, and mention the exact verification command you ran. "
58:            "If you edit files with apply_patch, paths are relative to the sandbox workspace root."
59:        ),
60:        default_manifest=Manifest(
61:            entries={
62:                "repo": LocalDir(src=HOST_REPO_DIR),
63:            }
64:        ),
65:        capabilities=Capabilities.default() + [
66:            Skills(
67:                lazy_from=LocalDirLazySkillSource(
68:                    # This is a host path read by the SDK process.
69:                    # Requested skills are copied into `skills_path` in the sandbox.
70:                    source=LocalDir(src=HOST_SKILLS_DIR),
71:                )
72:            ),
73:        ],
74:    )
75:
76:
77:async def main() -> None:
78:    result = await Runner.run(
79:        build_agent("gpt-5.5"),
80:        "Open `repo/task.md`, fix the issue, run the targeted test, and summarize the change.",
81:        run_config=RunConfig(
82:            sandbox=SandboxRunConfig(client=UnixLocalSandboxClient()),
83:            workflow_name="Sandbox coding example",
84:        ),
85:    )
86:    print(result.final_output)
87:
88:
89:if __name__ == "__main__":
90:    asyncio.run(main())
91:```
92:
93:See [examples/sandbox/docs/coding_task.py](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/examples/sandbox/docs/coding_task.py). It uses a tiny shell-based repo so the example can be verified deterministically across Unix-local runs.
94:
95:## Key choices
96:
97:Once the basic run works, the choices most people reach for next are:
98:
99:- `default_manifest`: the files, repos, directories, and mounts for fresh sandbox sessions
100:- `instructions`: short workflow rules that should apply across prompts
101:- `base_instructions`: an advanced escape hatch for replacing the SDK sandbox prompt
102:- `capabilities`: sandbox-native tools such as filesystem editing/image inspection, shell, skills, memory, and compaction
103:- `run_as`: the sandbox user identity for model-facing tools
104:- `SandboxRunConfig.client`: the sandbox backend
105:- `SandboxRunConfig.session`, `session_state`, or `snapshot`: how later runs reconnect to prior work
106:
107:## Where to go next
108:
109:- [Concepts](sandbox/guide.md): understand manifests, capabilities, permissions, snapshots, run config, and composition patterns.
110:- [Sandbox clients](sandbox/clients.md): choose Unix-local, Docker, hosted providers, and mount strategies.
111:- [Agent memory](sandbox/memory.md): preserve and reuse lessons from previous sandbox runs.
112:
113:If shell access is only one occasional tool, start with hosted shell in the [tools guide](tools.md). Reach for sandbox agents when workspace isolation, sandbox client choice, or sandbox-session resume behavior are part of the design.

.claude\rules\audit-action-loop.md:117:4. **Atomic batch** — bundle related edits (root + MEMORY.md close entry) in a single `git add ... && git commit` invocation to minimize cross-session bundling risk. Specifically: parallel sessions can commit during the gap between `git add` and `git commit`, and bundle your staged edit into their unrelated commit. The single-invocation form prevents this race.
.claude\rules\audit-action-loop.md:123:Audit-failure is the worst defect class: a broken audit looks like it's working (entries appear in JSONL) while providing 0 protection. Worse: a working audit that surfaces drift but isn't actioned has the same effect — the mechanization runs, the data accumulates, but nothing closes the drift. Within 12-24h of accumulation, drift becomes "background noise" that humans/agents stop checking. The audit-action-loop is the consumer-side discipline that makes wired audits valuable.
.claude\rules\audit-action-loop.md:130:- **Cross-session ownership unclear** — if working tree shows uncommitted changes from a parallel session, prefer `git stash` + commit + restore over editing in-place; minimizes bundling risk.

ccbp-claude-mcp-full\\n## Configuration\\r\\n\\r\\nMCP servers are configured in `.mcp.json` at the project root (project-scoped) or in `~/.claude.json` (user-scoped).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Server Types\\r\\n\\r\\n| Type | Transport | Example |\\r\\n|------|-----------|---------|\\r\\n| **stdio** | Spawns a local process | `npx`, `python`, binary |\\r\\n| **http** | Connects to a remote URL | \\\"remote-api\\\": {\\r\\n      \\\"type\\\": \\\"http\\\",\\r\\n      \\\"url\\\": \\\"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\\\"\\r\\n    }\\r\\n  }\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nUse environment variable `.claude/settings.json` control MCP server approval:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Key | Type | Description |\\r\\n|-----|------|-------------|\\r\\n| `enableAllProjectMcpServers` | boolean | Auto-approve all docs\realtime\guide.md:1:# Realtime agents guide
docs\realtime\guide.md:3:This guide explains how the OpenAI Agents SDK's realtime layer maps onto the OpenAI Realtime API, and what extra behavior the Python SDK adds on top.
docs\realtime\guide.md:7:    Realtime agents are in beta. Expect some breaking changes as we improve the implementation.
docs\realtime\guide.md:11:    If you want the default Python path, read the [quickstart](quickstart.md) first. If you are deciding whether your app should use server-side WebSocket or SIP, read [Realtime transport](transport.md). Browser WebRTC transport is not part of the Python SDK.
docs\realtime\guide.md:15:Realtime agents keep a long-lived connection open to the Realtime API so the model can process text and audio incrementally, stream audio output, call tools, and handle interruptions without restarting a fresh request on every turn.
docs\realtime\guide.md:19:-   **RealtimeAgent**: Instructions, tools, output guardrails, and handoffs for one realtime specialist
docs\realtime\guide.md:20:-   **RealtimeRunner**: Session factory that wires a starting agent to a realtime transport
docs\realtime\guide.md:21:-   **RealtimeSession**: A live session that sends input, receives events, tracks history, and executes tools
docs\realtime\guide.md:22:-   **RealtimeModel**: The transport abstraction. The default is OpenAI's server-side WebSocket implementation.
docs\realtime\guide.md:26:A typical realtime session looks like this:
docs\realtime\guide.md:28:1. Create one or more `RealtimeAgent`s.
docs\realtime\guide.md:29:2. Create a `RealtimeRunner` with the starting agent.
docs\realtime\guide.md:30:3. Call `await runner.run()` to get a `RealtimeSession`.
docs\realtime\guide.md:32:5. Send user input with `send_message()` or `send_audio()`.
docs\realtime\guide.md:37:By default, `RealtimeRunner` uses `OpenAIRealtimeWebSocketModel`, so the default Python path is a server-side WebSocket connection to the Realtime API. If you pass a different `RealtimeModel`, the same session lifecycle and agent features still apply, while the connection mechanics can change.
docs\realtime\guide.md:41:`RealtimeAgent` is intentionally narrower than the regular `Agent` type:
docs\realtime\guide.md:45:-   Voice can be configured, but it cannot change after the session has already produced spoken audio.

docs\voice\pipeline.md:3:[`VoicePipeline`][agents.voice.pipeline.VoicePipeline] is a class that makes it easy to turn your agentic workflows into a voice app. You pass in a workflow to run, and the pipeline takes care of transcribing input audio, detecting when the audio ends, calling your workflow at the right time, and turning the workflow output back into audio.

docs\voice\pipeline.md:44:You can run a pipeline via the [`run()`][agents.voice.pipeline.VoicePipeline.run] method, which lets you pass in audio input in two forms:
docs\voice\pipeline.md:46:1. [`AudioInput`][agents.voice.input.AudioInput] is used when you have a full audio transcript, and just want to produce a result for it. This is useful in cases where you don't need to detect when a speaker is done speaking; for example, when you have pre-recorded audio or in push-to-talk apps where it's clear when the user is done speaking.
docs\voice\pipeline.md:47:2. [`StreamedAudioInput`][agents.voice.input.StreamedAudioInput] is used when you might need to detect when a user is done speaking. It allows you to push audio chunks as they are detected, and the voice pipeline will automatically run the agent workflow at the right time, via a process called "activity detection".

docs\voice\pipeline.md:55:3. [`VoiceStreamEventError`][agents.voice.events.VoiceStreamEventError], is an error event.

docs\voice\pipeline.md:75:The Agents SDK currently does not provide any built-in interruption handling for [`StreamedAudioInput`][agents.voice.input.StreamedAudioInput]. Instead for every detected turn it will trigger a separate run of your workflow. If you want to handle interruptions inside your application you can listen to the [`VoiceStreamEventLifecycle`][agents.voice.events.VoiceStreamEventLifecycle] events. `turn_started` will indicate that a new turn was transcribed and processing is beginning. `turn_ended` will trigger after all the audio was dispatched for a respective turn. You could use these events to mute the microphone of the speaker when the model starts a turn and unmute it after you flushed all the related audio for a turn.

1:# Quickstart
2:
3:Realtime agents in the Python SDK are server-side, low-latency agents built on the OpenAI Realtime API over WebSocket transport.
4:
5:!!! warning "Beta feature"
6:
7:    Realtime agents are in beta. Expect some breaking changes as we improve the implementation.
8:
9:!!! note "Python SDK boundary"
10:
11:    The Python SDK does **not** provide a browser WebRTC transport. This page only covers Python-managed realtime sessions over server-side WebSockets. Use this SDK for server-side orchestration, tools, approvals, and telephony integrations. See also [Realtime transport](transport.md).
12:
13:## Prerequisites
14:
15:-   Python 3.10 or higher
16:-   OpenAI API key
17:-   Basic familiarity with the OpenAI Agents SDK
18:
19:## Installation
20:
21:If you haven't already, install the OpenAI Agents SDK:
22:
23:```bash
24:pip install openai-agents
25:```
26:
27:## Create a server-side realtime session
28:
29:### 1. Import the realtime components
30:
31:```python
32:import asyncio
33:
34:from agents.realtime import RealtimeAgent, RealtimeRunner
35:```
36:
37:### 2. Define the starting agent
38:
39:```python
40:agent = RealtimeAgent(
41:    name="Assistant",
42:    instructions="You are a helpful voice assistant. Keep responses short and conversational.",
43:)
44:```
45:
46:### 3. Configure the runner
47:
48:Prefer the nested `audio.input` / `audio.output` session settings shape for new code. For new realtime agents, start with `gpt-realtime-2`.
49:
50:```python
51:runner = RealtimeRunner(
52:    starting_agent=agent,
53:    config={
54:        "model_settings": {
55:            "model_name": "gpt-realtime-2",
56:            "audio": {
57:                "input": {
58:                    "format": "pcm16",
59:                    "transcription": {"model": "gpt-4o-mini-transcribe"},
60:                    "turn_detection": {
61:                        "type": "semantic_vad",
62:                        "interrupt_response": True,
63:                    },
64:                },
65:                "output": {
66:                    "format": "pcm16",
67:                    "voice": "ash",
68:                },
69:            },
70:        }
71:    },
72:)
73:```
74:
75:### 4. Start the session and send input
76:
77:`runner.run()` returns a `RealtimeSession`. The connection is opened when you enter the session context.
78:
79:```python
80:async def main() -> None:
81:    session = await runner.run()
82:
83:    async with session:
84:        await session.send_message("Say hello in one short sentence.")
85:
86:        async for event in session:
87:            if event.type == "audio":
88:                # Forward or play event.audio.data.
89:                pass
90:            elif event.type == "history_added":
91:                print(event.item)
92:            elif event.type == "agent_end":
93:                # One assistant turn finished.
94:                break
95:            elif event.type == "error":
96:                print(f"Error: {event.error}")
97:
98:
99:if __name__ == "__main__":
100:    asyncio.run(main())
101:```
102:
103:`session.send_message()` accepts either a plain string or a structured realtime message. For raw audio chunks, use [`session.send_audio()`][agents.realtime.session.RealtimeSession.send_audio].
104:
105:## What this quickstart does not include
106:
107:-   Microphone capture and speaker playback code. See the realtime examples in [`examples/realtime`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/realtime).
108:-   SIP / telephony attach flows. See [Realtime transport](transport.md) and the [SIP section](guide.md#sip-and-telephony).
109:
110:## Key settings
111:
112:Once the basic session works, the settings most people reach for next are:
113:
114:-   `model_name`
115:-   `audio.input.format`, `audio.output.format`
116:-   `audio.input.transcription`
117:-   `audio.input.noise_reduction`
118:-   `audio.input.turn_detection` for automatic turn detection
119:-   `audio.output.voice`
120:-   `tool_choice`, `prompt`, `tracing`
121:-   `async_tool_calls`, `guardrails_settings.debounce_text_length`, `tool_error_formatter`
122:
123:The older flat aliases such as `input_audio_format`, `output_audio_format`, `input_audio_transcription`, and `turn_detection` still work, but nested `audio` settings are preferred for new code.
124:
125:For manual turn control, use a raw `session.update` / `input_audio_buffer.commit` / `response.create` flow as described in the [Realtime agents guide](guide.md#manual-response-control).
126:
127:For the full schema, see [`RealtimeRunConfig`][agents.realtime.config.RealtimeRunConfig] and [`RealtimeSessionModelSettings`][agents.realtime.config.RealtimeSessionModelSettings].
128:
129:## Connection options
130:
131:Set your API key in the environment:
132:
133:```bash
134:export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-api-key-here"
135:```
136:
137:Or pass it directly when starting the session:
138:
139:```python
140:session = await runner.run(model_config={"api_key": "your-api-key"})
141:```
142:
143:`model_config` also supports:
144:
145:-   `url`: Custom WebSocket endpoint
146:-   `headers`: Custom request headers
147:-   `call_id`: Attach to an existing realtime call. In this repo, the documented attach flow is SIP.
148:-   `playback_tracker`: Report how much audio the user has actually heard
149:
150:If you pass `headers` explicitly, the SDK will **not** inject an `Authorization` header for you.
151:
152:When connecting to Azure OpenAI, pass a GA Realtime endpoint URL in `model_config["url"]` and explicit headers. Avoid the legacy beta path (`/openai/realtime?api-version=...`) with realtime agents. See the [Realtime agents guide](guide.md#low-level-access-and-custom-endpoints) for details.
153:

155:
156:-   Read [Realtime transport](transport.md) to choose between server-side WebSocket and SIP.
157:-   Read the [Realtime agents guide](guide.md) for lifecycle, structured input, approvals, handoffs, guardrails, and low-level control.
158:-   Browse the examples in [`examples/realtime`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/realtime).

1:# Realtime agents guide
2:
3:This guide explains how the OpenAI Agents SDK's realtime layer maps onto the OpenAI Realtime API, and what extra behavior the Python SDK adds on top.
4:
5:!!! warning "Beta feature"
6:
7:    Realtime agents are in beta. Expect some breaking changes as we improve the implementation.
8:
9:!!! note "Start here"
10:
11:    If you want the default Python path, read the [quickstart](quickstart.md) first. If you are deciding whether your app should use server-side WebSocket or SIP, read [Realtime transport](transport.md). Browser WebRTC transport is not part of the Python SDK.
12:
13:## Overview
14:
15:Realtime agents keep a long-lived connection open to the Realtime API so the model can process text and audio incrementally, stream audio output, call tools, and handle interruptions without restarting a fresh request on every turn.
16:
17:The main SDK components are:
18:
19:-   **RealtimeAgent**: Instructions, tools, output guardrails, and handoffs for one realtime specialist
20:-   **RealtimeRunner**: Session factory that wires a starting agent to a realtime transport
21:-   **RealtimeSession**: A live session that sends input, receives events, tracks history, and executes tools
22:-   **RealtimeModel**: The transport abstraction. The default is OpenAI's server-side WebSocket implementation.
23:
24:## Session lifecycle
25:
26:A typical realtime session looks like this:
27:
28:1. Create one or more `RealtimeAgent`s.
29:2. Create a `RealtimeRunner` with the starting agent.
30:3. Call `await runner.run()` to get a `RealtimeSession`.
31:4. Enter the session with `async with session:` or `await session.enter()`.
32:5. Send user input with `send_message()` or `send_audio()`.
33:6. Iterate over session events until the conversation ends.
34:
35:Unlike text-only runs, `runner.run()` does not produce a final result immediately. It returns a live session object that keeps local history, background tool execution, guardrail state, and the active agent configuration in sync with the transport layer.
36:
37:By default, `RealtimeRunner` uses `OpenAIRealtimeWebSocketModel`, so the default Python path is a server-side WebSocket connection to the Realtime API. If you pass a different `RealtimeModel`, the same session lifecycle and agent features still apply, while the connection mechanics can change.
38:
39:## Agent and session configuration
40:
41:`RealtimeAgent` is intentionally narrower than the regular `Agent` type:
42:
43:-   Model choice is configured at the session level, not per agent.
44:-   Structured outputs are not supported.
45:-   Voice can be configured, but it cannot change after the session has already produced spoken audio.
46:-   Instructions, function tools, handoffs, hooks, and output guardrails all still work.
47:
48:`RealtimeSessionModelSettings` supports both a newer nested `audio` config and older flat aliases. Prefer the nested shape for new code, and start with `gpt-realtime-2` for new realtime agents:
49:
50:```python
51:runner = RealtimeRunner(
52:    starting_agent=agent,
53:    config={
54:        "model_settings": {
55:            "model_name": "gpt-realtime-2",
56:            "audio": {
57:                "input": {
58:                    "format": "pcm16",
272:The Python SDK includes a first-class SIP attach flow via [`OpenAIRealtimeSIPModel`][agents.realtime.openai_realtime.OpenAIRealtimeSIPModel].
273:
274:Use it when a call arrives through the Realtime Calls API and you want to attach an agent session to the resulting `call_id`:
275:
276:```python
277:from agents.realtime import RealtimeRunner
278:from agents.realtime.openai_realtime import OpenAIRealtimeSIPModel
279:
280:runner = RealtimeRunner(starting_agent=agent, model=OpenAIRealtimeSIPModel())
281:
282:async with await runner.run(
283:    model_config={
284:        "call_id": call_id_from_webhook,
285:    }
286:) as session:
287:    async for event in session:
288:        ...
289:```
290:
291:If you need to accept the call first and want the accept payload to match the agent-derived session configuration, use `OpenAIRealtimeSIPModel.build_initial_session_payload(...)`. The complete flow is shown in [`examples/realtime/twilio_sip/server.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/realtime/twilio_sip/server.py).
292:
293:## Low-level access and custom endpoints
294:
295:You can access the underlying transport object through `session.model`.
296:
297:Use this when you need:
298:
299:-   custom listeners via `session.model.add_listener(...)`
300:-   raw client events such as `response.create` or `session.update`
301:-   custom `url`, `headers`, or `api_key` handling through `model_config`
302:-   `call_id` attach to an existing realtime call
303:
304:`RealtimeModelConfig` supports:
305:
306:-   `api_key`
307:-   `url`
308:-   `headers`
309:-   `initial_model_settings`
310:-   `playback_tracker`
311:-   `call_id`
312:
313:This repository's shipped `call_id` example is SIP. The broader Realtime API also uses `call_id` for some server-side control flows, but those are not packaged as Python examples here.
314:
315:When connecting to Azure OpenAI, pass a GA Realtime endpoint URL and explicit headers. For example:
316:
317:```python
318:session = await runner.run(
319:    model_config={
320:        "url": "wss://<your-resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/realtime?model=<deployment-name>",
321:        "headers": {"api-key": "<your-azure-api-key>"},
322:    }
323:)
324:```
325:
326:For token-based authentication, use a bearer token in `headers`:
327:
328:```python
329:session = await runner.run(
330:    model_config={
331:        "url": "wss://<your-resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/realtime?model=<deployment-name>",
332:        "headers": {"authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
333:    }
334:)
335:```
336:
337:If you pass `headers`, the SDK does not add `Authorization` automatically. Avoid the legacy beta path (`/openai/realtime?api-version=...`) with realtime agents.
338:

340:
341:-   [Realtime transport](transport.md)
342:-   [Quickstart](quickstart.md)
343:-   [OpenAI Realtime conversations](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-conversations/)
344:-   [OpenAI Realtime server-side controls](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-server-controls/)
345:-   [`examples/realtime`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/realtime)

1:# Realtime transport
2:
3:Use this page to decide how realtime agents fit into your Python application.
4:
5:!!! note "Python SDK boundary"
6:
7:    The Python SDK does **not** include a browser WebRTC transport. This page is only about Python SDK transport choices: server-side WebSockets and SIP attach flows. Browser WebRTC is a separate platform topic, documented in the official [Realtime API with WebRTC](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-webrtc/) guide.
8:
9:## Decision guide
10:
11:| Goal | Start with | Why |
12:| --- | --- | --- |
13:| Build a server-managed realtime app | [Quickstart](quickstart.md) | The default Python path is a server-side WebSocket session managed by `RealtimeRunner`. |
14:| Understand which transport and deployment shape to choose | This page | Use this before you commit to a transport or deployment shape. |
15:| Attach agents to phone or SIP calls | [Realtime guide](guide.md) and [`examples/realtime/twilio_sip`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/realtime/twilio_sip) | The repo ships a SIP attach flow driven by `call_id`. |
16:
17:## Server-side WebSocket is the default Python path
18:
19:`RealtimeRunner` uses `OpenAIRealtimeWebSocketModel` unless you pass a custom `RealtimeModel`.
20:
21:That means the standard Python topology looks like this:
22:
23:1. Your Python service creates a `RealtimeRunner`.
24:2. `await runner.run()` returns a `RealtimeSession`.
25:3. Enter the session and send text, structured messages, or audio.
26:4. Consume `RealtimeSessionEvent` items and forward audio or transcripts to your application.
27:
28:This is the topology used by the core demo app, the CLI example, and the Twilio Media Streams example:
29:
30:-   [`examples/realtime/app`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/realtime/app)
31:-   [`examples/realtime/cli`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/realtime/cli)
32:-   [`examples/realtime/twilio`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/realtime/twilio)
33:
34:Use this path when your server owns the audio pipeline, tool execution, approval flow, and history handling.
35:
36:## SIP attach is the telephony path
37:
38:For the telephony flow documented in this repository, the Python SDK attaches to an existing realtime call via `call_id`.
39:
40:This topology looks like:
41:
42:1. OpenAI sends your service a webhook such as `realtime.call.incoming`.
43:2. Your service accepts the call through the Realtime Calls API.
44:3. Your Python service starts a `RealtimeRunner(..., model=OpenAIRealtimeSIPModel())`.
45:4. The session connects with `model_config={"call_id": ...}` and then processes events like any other realtime session.
46:
47:This is the topology shown in [`examples/realtime/twilio_sip`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/realtime/twilio_sip).
48:
49:The broader Realtime API also uses `call_id` for some server-side control patterns, but this repository's shipped attach example is SIP.
50:
51:## Browser WebRTC is outside this SDK
52:
53:If your app's primary client is a browser using Realtime WebRTC:
54:
55:-   Treat it as outside the scope of the Python SDK docs in this repository.
56:-   Use the official [Realtime API with WebRTC](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-webrtc/) and [Realtime conversations](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-conversations/) docs for the client-side flow and event model.
57:-   Use the official [Realtime server-side controls](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-server-controls/) guide if you need a sideband server connection on top of a browser WebRTC client.
58:-   Do not expect this repository to provide a browser-side `RTCPeerConnection` abstraction or a ready-made browser WebRTC sample.
59:
60:This repository also does not currently ship a browser WebRTC plus Python sideband example.
61:
62:## Custom endpoints and attach points
63:
64:The transport configuration surface in [`RealtimeModelConfig`][agents.realtime.model.RealtimeModelConfig] lets you adapt the default paths:
65:
66:-   `url`: Override the WebSocket endpoint
67:-   `headers`: Provide explicit headers such as Azure auth headers
68:-   `api_key`: Pass an API key directly or via callback
69:-   `call_id`: Attach to an existing realtime call. In this repository, the documented example is SIP.
70:-   `playback_tracker`: Report actual playback progress for interruption handling
71:
72:See the [Realtime agents guide](guide.md) for the detailed lifecycle and capability surface once you've chosen a topology.

docs\release.md:24:In this version, sandbox local source materialization keeps `LocalFile.src` and `LocalDir.src` within the materialization `base_dir` unless the source path is covered by `Manifest.extra_path_grants`. The `base_dir` is the SDK process current working directory when the manifest is applied; relative local sources are resolved from that directory, while absolute local sources must already be inside it or under an explicit grant. This closes a local artifact boundary issue, but it can affect applications that intentionally copy trusted host files or directories from outside that base directory into a sandbox workspace.

1:# OpenAI Agents SDK [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/openai-agents?label=pypi%20package)](https://pypi.org/project/openai-agents/)
2:
3:The OpenAI Agents SDK is a lightweight yet powerful framework for building multi-agent workflows. It is provider-agnostic, supporting the OpenAI Responses and Chat Completions APIs, as well as 100+ other LLMs.
4:
5:<img src="https://cdn.openai.com/API/docs/images/orchestration.png" alt="Image of the Agents Tracing UI" style="max-height: 803px;">
6:
7:> [!NOTE]
8:> Looking for the JavaScript/TypeScript version? Check out [Agents SDK JS/TS](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-js).
9:
10:### Core concepts:
11:
12:1. [**Agents**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/agents): LLMs configured with instructions, tools, guardrails, and handoffs
13:1. [**Sandbox Agents**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/sandbox_agents): Agents preconfigured to work with a container to perform work over long time horizons.
14:1. **[Agents as tools](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tools/#agents-as-tools) / [Handoffs](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/)**: Delegating to other agents for specific tasks
15:1. [**Tools**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tools/): Various Tools let agents take actions (functions, MCP, hosted tools)
16:1. [**Guardrails**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/guardrails/): Configurable safety checks for input and output validation
17:1. [**Human in the loop**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/human_in_the_loop/): Built-in mechanisms for involving humans across agent runs
18:1. [**Sessions**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/sessions/): Automatic conversation history management across agent runs
19:1. [**Tracing**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tracing/): Built-in tracking of agent runs, allowing you to view, debug and optimize your workflows
20:1. [**Realtime Agents**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/realtime/quickstart/): Build powerful voice agents with `gpt-realtime-2` and full agent features
21:
22:Explore the [examples](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples) directory to see the SDK in action, and read our [documentation](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/) for more details.

49:## Run your first Sandbox Agent
50:
51:[Sandbox Agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/sandbox_agents) are new in version 0.14.0. A sandbox agent is an agent that uses a computer environment to perform real work with a filesystem, in an environment you configure and control. Sandbox agents are useful when the agent needs to inspect files, run commands, apply patches, or carry workspace state across longer tasks.
52:
53:```python
54:from agents import Runner
55:from agents.run import RunConfig
56:from agents.sandbox import Manifest, SandboxAgent, SandboxRunConfig
57:from agents.sandbox.entries import GitRepo
58:from agents.sandbox.sandboxes import UnixLocalSandboxClient
59:
60:agent = SandboxAgent(
61:    name="Workspace Assistant",
62:    instructions="Inspect the sandbox workspace before answering.",
63:    default_manifest=Manifest(
64:        entries={
65:            "repo": GitRepo(repo="openai/openai-agents-python", ref="main"),
66:        }
67:    ),
68:)
69:
70:result = Runner.run_sync(
71:    agent,
72:    "Inspect the repo README and summarize what this project does.",
73:    # Run this agent on the local filesystem
74:    run_config=RunConfig(sandbox=SandboxRunConfig(client=UnixLocalSandboxClient())),
75:)
76:print(result.final_output)
77:
78:# This project provides a Python SDK for building multi-agent workflows.
79:```
